newsitem.title: USA: US LINE-ITEM VETO OF TAX RULE HITS FINANCE SECTOR.
newsitem.headline: US LINE-ITEM VETO OF TAX RULE HITS FINANCE SECTOR.

text.p: U.S. financial companies found themselves in select company on Monday as President Bill Clinton exercised one of the first three line-item vetoes on a tax provision benefitting banks, insurance companies and securities firms with overseas operations.

The tax provision, estimated to have cost the government $317 million over five years, would have allowed companies to avoid paying immediate U.S. taxes on financing income earned overseas like interest, dividends and certain capital gains.
Clinton said the provision allowed "the avoidance of federal taxation in an inappropriate way."
U.S. corporations generally do not pay income tax on profits from their overseas subsidiaries until the money is brought back to the United States.

But in 1986 Congress curtailed the deferral on concerns that financial companies could be shifting income earned in the United States to foreign subsidiaries in countries that did not collect income tax.
Under the 1986 law, U.S. companies owed immediate taxes on income earned overseas from active financing activities.
The Securities Industry Association had strongly backed undoing the 1986 rule.
"The President's veto fails to recognize the challenges faced by U.S. firms in foreign markets," SIA spokesman Jim Spellman said. "The markets are increasingly global."

Using the newly granted line item veto authority for the first time on Monday, President Clinton said he would also veto a provision giving a tax break to food processing companies and a Medicaid measure benefitting New York State.
Several lawmakers previously challenged the line item veto law on constitutional grounds but the Supreme Court ruled that the legislators lacked standing to sue prior to the veto being used.
